title: Trust Structures for Asset Protection: Strategies and Examples
summary: How asset protection trusts work, which trust structures may shield assets from creditors and lawsuits, and what legal and tax limits apply.
body_markdown:
Trusts can help protect wealth from creditors, lawsuits and financial problems that beneficiaries may encounter, but not every trust provides the same level of protection. The result depends on how the trust is structured, who controls the assets, when the trust is established and which state’s laws apply. Some arrangements can help shield assets from future claims, while others offer little protection at all. The key is matching the trust structure to the specific risks and goals you are trying to address.


[A financial advisor can help you evaluate](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=truststructuresforassetprotection) **how trusts, investment accounts and other assets may work together to support your long-term goals.**


## How Trusts Can Protect Assets


Trusts can help protect assets from creditors, lawsuits and other financial risks by separating ownership and control of property. When you establish a trust, you transfer assets to a trustee who manages them for the benefit of designated individuals, known as beneficiaries. The person who creates and funds the trust is the grantor.


The level of protection depends largely on the[type of trust](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/types-of-trusts) . A revocable living trust generally doesn’t protect assets from the grantor’s creditors because the grantor retains control and can modify or cancel the arrangement. An irrevocable trust, however, may provide stronger protection. This is because the grantor typically gives up certain ownership rights and control over the property.


Some trusts may also include[spendthrift provisions](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/spendthrift-trust) . These generally prevent beneficiaries from transferring their interests or creditors from claiming trust assets before they’re distributed. Discretionary trusts offer another layer of protection by allowing the trustee to decide when and how much money beneficiaries receive, rather than giving beneficiaries automatic access to the funds.


However, putting assets into a trust doesn’t automatically protect them from creditors. The trust must be properly structured under applicable state laws, and certain creditors may still have legal claims against trust assets. Protection also depends on when the trust was established, particularly if the grantor already faced debts or potential lawsuits when transferring the property.


## Trust Structures Used for Asset Protection


Different types of trusts provide different levels of asset protection, depending on who owns the assets, who benefits from them and the laws governing the trust. Some trusts protect inheritances from creditors. Meanwhile, others help shield personal wealth from lawsuits or preserve assets for long-term care planning:


- Third-party[irrevocable trusts](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/irrevocable-trust) are commonly used to protect assets left to children or other beneficiaries. These trusts commonly include spendthrift provisions that restrict creditors from accessing assets before they’re distributed.
- [Discretionary trusts](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/discretionary-trust) provide similar protection by allowing a trustee to determine when and how much beneficiaries receive.
- [Domestic asset protection trusts (DAPTs)](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/domestic-asset-protection-trusts-estate-planning) allow individuals to transfer assets into certain irrevocable trusts while remaining beneficiaries. These arrangements are permitted in states such as Nevada, Delaware, Alaska and South Dakota, although protection varies by state.
- Offshore asset protection trusts operate under foreign laws and may offer additional creditor protections, but they typically involve higher costs and complex legal and tax reporting requirements.
- [Spousal lifetime access trusts (SLATs)](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/spousal-lifetime-access-trust) allow one spouse to transfer assets into an irrevocable trust benefiting the other spouse. This can provide some indirect access to family wealth while potentially protecting assets from certain creditors. However, divorce or the beneficiary spouse’s death can eliminate that access.
- Medicaid asset protection trusts may help older adults preserve assets while planning for future long-term care expenses, provided they satisfy Medicaid’s eligibility and transfer rules.
- Special needs trusts help individuals with disabilities receive financial support without necessarily jeopardizing eligibility for means-tested government benefits.


No single trust works for every situation. The appropriate structure depends on your financial goals, potential creditor exposure, family circumstances and state laws.

## Examples of Asset Protection Trusts in Practice


The benefits of asset protection trusts become clearer when considering how they might function in different financial situations. The following examples are hypothetical and assume that each trust complies with applicable state and federal laws.


To start, consider a parent who wants to leave $750,000 to an adult child with outstanding debts. Instead of distributing the inheritance outright, the parent establishes a third-party irrevocable trust with spendthrift provisions. The trustee[manages the inheritance](https://smartasset.com/investing/how-does-inheritance-work) and makes distributions under the trust agreement, generally preventing ordinary creditors from reaching assets that remain protected inside the trust.


Consider another example, involving a physician with $2 million in investment assets who wants protection against potential future lawsuits. Years before any claim arises, the physician establishes a properly structured DAPT in a state that permits these arrangements. Although certain future creditors may face restrictions on accessing the trust assets, the protection isn’t absolute. It may face challenges under bankruptcy or other applicable laws.


Finally, let’s take a look at an example for a 68-year-old homeowner who transfers a $400,000 residence into a[Medicaid asset protection trust](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/medicaid-trust) . If properly structured and funded sufficiently early, the arrangement may help preserve the home when the owner eventually needs long-term nursing home care. However, Medicaid generally reviews transfers made within the preceding 60 months under 42 U.S.C. Section 1396p.1


These examples illustrate why timing, jurisdiction and the beneficiary’s rights matter as much as the value of the assets transferred.


## Limits Courts and Laws Place on Protection


While asset protection trusts can help shield wealth from creditors, they don’t provide absolute protection. Courts can challenge certain transfers. Further, state and federal laws may allow creditors to recover assets under specific circumstances. The level of protection depends on the trust’s structure, the timing of transfers and applicable laws.


One major limitation involves fraudulent or voidable transfers. Under state laws based on the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, creditors may challenge transfers made to hinder, delay or defraud them. For example,[transferring property into a trust](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/how-to-transfer-property-into-a-trust) after being sued may not prevent creditors from pursuing those assets.


Federal bankruptcy law also imposes restrictions. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 548(e), a bankruptcy trustee may recover certain transfers into self-settled trusts made within 10 years before a bankruptcy filing if the debtor intended to hinder, delay or defraud creditors.2


Certain obligations may also override trust protections. Depending on state law, creditors seeking unpaid child support, government tax debts or other qualifying claims may still reach trust assets.


## Costs and Tradeoffs to Weigh


Asset protection trusts can help preserve wealth, but they also come with costs and restrictions. Establishing an irrevocable trust generally requires giving up significant control over transferred assets, potentially limiting your ability to access funds for retirement, healthcare or unexpected expenses. Depending on the trust’s terms, changing beneficiaries or modifying distribution instructions may also be difficult.


Setting up and maintaining a trust can be expensive. Attorney fees, professional trustee compensation and ongoing administrative expenses can add up over time. Certain trusts must also file separate income tax returns using[IRS Form 1041](https://smartasset.com/taxes/all-about-irs-form-1041) , creating additional reporting obligations and potential tax liabilities.


Another consideration is the potential loss of a[step-up in cost basis](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/stepped-up-basis) . Under IRS Revenue Ruling 2023-2, certain assets held in irrevocable trusts that are excluded from the grantor’s taxable estate generally don’t receive a basis adjustment at death.3 This could leave beneficiaries facing larger capital gains taxes when selling appreciated investments.


Finally, timing plays a major role in how effectively a trust protects assets. Transfers made after a lawsuit arises or when substantial debts already exist face challenges and even reversals by creditors. Establishing and funding a properly structured trust well before financial problems emerge generally provides stronger protection.


## Bottom Line


Asset protection trusts can provide meaningful safeguards against future creditors, lawsuits and financial risks when established early and structured correctly. However, they cannot reliably shield assets from debts or claims that already exist.
